---
title: "An AI SRE that cites evidence you can re-run"
subtitle: "Firebreak investigates a production incident, names a cause or refuses to, and links every sentence to the query behind it."
---

## The problem

The expensive part of an incident is not the fix. It is the twenty minutes spent deciding
which of forty services to look at, made from dashboards under time pressure, by someone who
was asleep.

Two things go wrong in that twenty minutes, and they pull in opposite directions:

| What goes wrong | Why the obvious fix makes it worse |
|---|---|
| The service that pages you is rarely the service that broke | An agent that answers faster gives you a confident wrong service sooner |
| The reasoning is lost by the time the postmortem is written | An agent that writes prose produces a postmortem nobody can check |

So the design question is not *how do we answer more often*. A confident wrong answer costs
more than no answer, because it sends people to the wrong dashboard and teaches them to
distrust the tool. The question is:

> How do you make an answer **checkable**, and how do you get the system to **say nothing**
> when the evidence will not support saying something?

## What Firebreak does

Four commitments, each of which costs something real.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Deterministic first

Robust anomaly scores and a ranked service list are computed **before any model runs**, using
a median and median absolute deviation rather than a mean and standard deviation, because one
spike moves a mean and a fault is a spike.

If nothing scores above the abstention threshold, the investigation ends there. On a healthy
system the cheapest correct answer is to stop.

**The cost:** the model starts from a shortlist it did not choose, so a fault the statistics
miss is a fault the agent never sees.

### Evidence or nothing

Every tool call records its query, its time window, a fingerprint of the backend it hit, and a
hash of the rows that came back. A claim cites those records by id.

A model never writes a query string. Tools take validated arguments and build their own
queries.

**The cost:** flexibility. The agent can only ask the fourteen questions somebody wrote a tool
for.

### A gate that removes claims

Six checks run on the finished report, including re-executing every citation and comparing the
hash. A claim that fails is **removed**, not annotated, because a warning beside a claim is a
claim that still gets quoted.

**The cost:** a report can come back thinner than the investigation was.

### Abstention as a real answer

On a healthy system it says so, names the largest deviation it found and the threshold it was
compared against, and stops.

**The cost:** it abstains on real faults too. On the recordings available the deterministic
baseline gets the abstention call right {{< var recorded_abstention_correct >}} times out of
{{< var recorded_abstention_trials >}}, which is the largest open problem in the project.
:::

## What one investigation looks like

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  B["Incident bundle<br/><small>frozen replay</small>"] --> T["Triage<br/><small>no model</small>"]
  T -->|"nothing unusual"| A["Abstain<br/><small>with the threshold it failed</small>"]
  T -->|"ranked shortlist"| L["Agent loop<br/><small>commander, 4 specialists,<br/>critic, budgeted</small>"]
  L --> G["Exit gate<br/><small>6 checks</small>"]
  G -->|"claims survive"| R["Report<br/><small>every claim cited</small>"]
  G -->|"support too thin"| A
```

Triage can end the investigation on its own, before a model is involved. That is the path a
no-fault incident takes, and it costs nothing.

## What is actually built

| | |
|---|---|
| **Scenario library** | {{< var specs >}} fault-injection specs across four splits |
| **Recorded incidents** | Neither held-out test split has any recordings. They ship as a release asset, not in this repository |
| **Offline demo** | {{< var showcase_incidents >}} incidents replayed from {{< var showcase_cassettes >}} recorded answers, no model and no network |
| **Tools** | 14, each typed and capped, each recording its own provenance |
| **Decision records** | {{< var adrs >}}, each with the alternatives it rejected |
| **Tests** | {{< var tests_passed >}} passing, {{< var coverage_percent >}}% coverage against an exact floor |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where these numbers come from

Every one is generated by `scripts/build_site_stats.py` into `explainer/_variables.yml`, from a
file under `reports/`. No page on this site types a figure, and a figure that file does not carry
is one no page may state. A count of recorded bundles is deliberately absent: it describes
whichever machine ran the build, since `bundles/` is git-ignored.
:::

## How well does it work

Honestly: that is not measured yet, and this page will not show you a number it cannot stand
behind.

Firebreak is built and tested end to end, and so is its evaluation harness. The harness is
currently reporting that it has nothing quotable to say, which is the harness working rather
than failing. `reports/eval/` holds eight reports, every one marked
`quotable_as_a_result: false` with its reason attached, and the build refuses to publish a figure
from any of them.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two of those figures look excellent and are not

One is a run over synthetic fixtures. One is a partly recorded split that was also used for
tuning. Either would make a good screenshot, and publishing either would be the project's own
honesty rule broken in its own interface, so the build will not do it.

The one comparison worth having is on [Measurement](metrics.qmd): the same deterministic triage
names nearly every fault on fixtures and {{< var recorded_root_cause_correct >}} of
{{< var recorded_root_cause_applicable >}} on real recordings. Fixtures are a different scale of
difficulty, not an easier version of the same thing, and that gap is the single most useful thing
this project has learned.
:::

Two inputs turn this into numbers, and neither is an engineering task: **model credentials**, and
**recordings for the held-out splits**. After those, `make eval` and `make site-stats` fill every
surface here with no template edited, because the pages are built so a stated absence becomes a
stated figure the moment its report says it may be quoted. [What is next](next.qmd) has the
order.

## Try it

Runs on a clone with no model, no Docker and no network:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hoomanesteki/firebreak-ai-sre-agent.git
cd firebreak-ai-sre-agent
make setup
make demo      # chooses live or offline, and says which
make console   # six pages on http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

`make demo` replays ten incidents rebuilt from their scenario specs and checks each against
its recording. Two of the ten abstain, which is the right answer for them.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The demo's numbers are better than the real ones

It replays a deterministic stub rather than a model, and it prints that before its first line.
It names every fault in the set. The same triage, measured on real recordings, names
{{< var recorded_root_cause_correct >}} of {{< var recorded_root_cause_applicable >}}. The demo
shows that the whole path runs and reproduces. It says nothing about quality.
:::
